title: Breaking Certified Defenses: Semantic Adversarial Examples with Spoofed Robustness Certificates
authors: Amin Ghiasi, Ali Shafahi, Tom Goldstein

pages.title: When the Certificate Lies
pages.subtitle: Provable robustness that proves the wrong thing

blocks.html: Certified defenses promise something the usual heuristic defenses cannot: not just “we tried hard and could not break it,” but a genuine mathematical guarantee that no adversarial example exists within a given distance of the input. For each prediction the defense emits a certificate — a radius $r$ inside which the label is provably constant. It feels like the end of the adversarial arms race: a proof is a proof.

This paper shows the proof can be made to vouch for an image that is obviously wrong. The authors construct what they call a Shadow Attack: they produce inputs that are large and clearly altered to a human eye — recolored, with a faint colored haze laid over the object — yet still arrive carrying a valid, large robustness certificate, and are misclassified. The certificate’s math is correct. It is simply answering a question nobody should have been comforted by.

The intuition for why this is possible: certificates are proven against a specific threat model, almost always small perturbations bounded in an $\ell_p$ norm (every pixel changes by at most some tiny $\epsilon$). The certificate is completely silent about perturbations outside that ball. A real attacker is not obligated to stay inside the box — so the attack steps far outside it, in a direction the certifier still happens to bless.

The punchline: you can build a visibly, semantically altered image that the network misclassifies while the defense certifies it as robust with a large radius. The guarantee is technically true and practically meaningless — a “spoofed” certificate.

Figure 1 of the paper makes it vivid: a natural macaw is shown alongside a Shadow Attack version that any person still reads as a macaw, mildly tinted — but the model labels it “bucket” and stamps it with a certificate larger than the one the genuine clean image received.
Start with what a certified classifier really promises. It guarantees that its prediction is constant within an $\ell_p$ ball of radius $r$ around the input. Formally:

Term by term: $x$ is the input image; $f$ is the classifier; $\delta$ is any candidate perturbation; $\|\delta\|_p$ is its size measured in the $\ell_p$ norm (e.g. $\ell_2$ is Euclidean length, $\ell_\infty$ is the largest single-pixel change); and $r$ is the certified radius. The statement reads: for every perturbation no larger than $r$, the predicted label does not change. This is genuinely proven — no white-box or black-box attack exists inside that ball.

The catch hides in the phrase “measured in the $\ell_p$ norm.” An $\ell_p$ ball counts change pixel by pixel, numerically. But many edits that a human perceives as “the same object” move every pixel by a large amount. Shift the whole image one pixel to the right and every edge jumps; rotate the hue and every color value changes; lay a smooth tint over the scene and the entire image drifts. All of these have enormous $\ell_p$ distance, so they sit far outside the certified ball, where the certificate makes no claim whatsoever.

So the exploitable flaw is the gap between two notions of “close”: perceptual similarity (does it still look like the same scene to a person?) versus $\ell_p$ distance (did the raw pixel numbers stay close?). The whole defense is built on assuming these coincide. They do not.

pages.title: Randomized Smoothing & CROWN-IBP
pages.subtitle: The two certified defenses under attack

blocks.html: The paper targets the two leading families of certified defense, so it is worth knowing roughly how each issues its certificate.

Randomized smoothing (Cohen et al., 2019) turns any base classifier into a certified one by adding Gaussian noise. To classify $x$, you sample many noisy copies $x + \eta$ with $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ and take a majority vote. The certified $\ell_2$ radius grows with how lopsided that vote is — the more confidently the noisy votes agree on one class, the larger the certificate:

Here $\sigma$ is the noise level; $\underline{p_A}$ is a lower bound on the probability the smoothed classifier votes for the top class $A$; $\overline{p_B}$ is an upper bound on the runner-up class $B$; and $\Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse standard-normal CDF (the “z-score” function). The lesson to keep: the radius is large precisely when the noisy votes are overwhelmingly one class. The attack’s job is to find a visibly altered image whose noisy copies still vote almost unanimously for a wrong class.

CROWN-IBP (Zhang et al., 2020) is a deterministic certifier for $\ell_\infty$ robustness. It propagates interval bounds through the network to prove that no $\ell_\infty$ perturbation up to $\epsilon$ can change the output. The Shadow Attack spoofs it too, showing the weakness is not specific to one certification mechanism but to the shared $\ell_p$ threat-model assumption.

pages.title: The Shadow Attack Objective
pages.subtitle: Make a big perturbation that still looks natural

blocks.html: The Shadow Attack does not add tiny pixel noise (the very thing certificates are designed to resist). It deliberately searches for a large perturbation $\delta$ that (a) flips the label and (b) looks natural enough that the certifier still hands out a big certificate. The key realization: certificates do not penalize a perturbation for being large in $\ell_p$ — they penalize it for being detectable as adversarial. So if you make the perturbation big but smooth, dull, and uniform across color channels, it reads to the certifier like a benign lighting change rather than an attack.
Concretely the attacker maximizes the misclassification loss over $\delta$ while paying three penalties that keep $\delta$ photographically plausible:

Reading the four pieces. $L_{\text{spoof}}$ is the attack’s classification loss — pushing the perturbed image $x+\delta$ to be misclassified (and, for smoothing, to be misclassified even under added Gaussian noise, which is what spoofs the certificate). $C(\delta)$ penalizes the overall magnitude of the perturbation per channel. $TV(\delta)$ is the total variation — the sum of differences between neighboring pixels; penalizing it forces $\delta$ to be smooth (no high-frequency speckle, which is the tell-tale signature of an adversarial example). $\text{Dissim}(\delta)$ penalizes the perturbation differing across the red/green/blue channels, so the change looks like a uniform tint rather than colored noise. The $\lambda$’s weight each penalty.

The combined effect is a perturbation that is large in $\ell_p$ but perceptually reads as a gentle, smooth, single-color haze — a “shadow” cast over the image. To a person it is clearly the same object under a tint; to the pixel-counting norm it is huge; and crucially, to the certifier it looks robust.

pages.title: How the Certificate Gets Spoofed
pages.subtitle: A true theorem about the wrong neighborhood

blocks.html: Why do smooth, low-saturation, channel-uniform perturbations earn large certificates? Recall the randomized-smoothing radius grows with how unanimously the noisy votes agree. The three penalties are precisely designed to make the perturbed image robust to the certifier’s own Gaussian noise: a smooth, uniform tint shifts the whole image consistently, so adding noise on top still leaves nearly every sample voting for the (wrong) target class. The vote stays lopsided, $\underline{p_A}$ stays high, and the certificate comes out large — often larger than the genuine image’s.

It is essential to see that nothing in the certificate’s proof is broken. The certifier honestly computes: “around this input $x' = x+\delta$, every $\ell_p$ perturbation up to radius $r$ keeps the label.” That statement is true. The deception lives entirely in what the certificate is silent about: the large semantic move from the original $x$ to $x'$ was never an $\ell_p$ perturbation within $r$, so the proof never covered it. A user who reads “certified robust” as “this is the right answer on a faithful image” has been misled.
A correct proof about an irrelevant ball is still a misleading guarantee. Robustness is only meaningful relative to a threat model that matches the perturbations a real adversary will actually use.

Operationally, the attacker runs the optimization above for a few hundred steps, tuning the $\lambda$ penalties so the result both misclassifies and emerges with a valid, non-trivial certificate — manufacturing the paradoxical artifact of a confidently “certified” wrong answer on an obviously edited picture.

pages.title: Certified and Wrong at the Same Time
pages.subtitle: Spoofing randomized smoothing on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet

blocks.html: The headline experiment attacks randomized smoothing on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. For each test image the authors craft a Shadow Attack version, then ask the smoothed classifier to certify it. The result: the spoofed images receive certificates that are not just valid but, on average, larger than the certificates of the unmodified, correctly-classified images — while being misclassified.

In the paper’s Table 1, on CIFAR-10 the mean Shadow-Attack certified radius exceeds the mean radius of the natural/correct images, and similarly on ImageNet. So a defender ranking images by “how robust is this prediction” would rank the adversarial ones as more trustworthy than the clean ones. The visualizations (Figure 2) show the attack images as plainly the same object under a faint colored shadow.

blocks.html: An ablation (removing one component to measure its contribution) confirms each penalty matters: dropping the total-variation term makes $\delta$ speckly and the certifier no longer cooperates; dropping the channel-similarity term lets colored noise creep in and shrinks the spoofed radius. The smoothness and color penalties are what convert a normal adversarial example into a certificate-spoofing one.

pages.title: Spoofing CROWN-IBP & The Lesson
pages.subtitle: Match the threat model to reality

blocks.html: The same idea spoofs CROWN-IBP, the deterministic $\ell_\infty$ certifier. The attacker simply constrains $\delta$ to stay within the small $\ell_\infty$ budget the certifier checks while still applying the smoothness and color penalties, again producing misclassified images that emerge certified. That the trick generalizes across a randomized certifier and a deterministic one shows the weakness is in the shared assumption, not in any single proof technique.

The paper is emphatically not an argument against certified defenses — it is a warning about how to interpret them. A certificate is a conditional promise: “safe, assuming the only attacks are small $\ell_p$ perturbations.” When that assumption fails, the promise is hollow, and worse, it is actively misleading because it wears the authority of a proof.
Robustness certificates are only as trustworthy as their threat model. Certifying against $\ell_p$ noise does not certify against color, geometry, or any perturbation the norm cannot see.

The constructive takeaway is to broaden threat models — certify against semantic transformations (recoloring, translation, rotation, blur) directly — and to report clearly which perturbations a certificate does and does not cover. Within this collection the paper sits beside the test-time attacks (FGSM, PGD, the adversarial patch) and the unrestricted-adversarial line of work: all of them escape the tidy $\ell_p$ ball, and all of them argue that “provably robust” means nothing until you pin down provably robust against what.
